steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. MARL / stochastic games
- MARL: learning dynamics of strategic agents in shared environment; frontier of ML and control
- stochastic games = Markov games: multi-agent generalization of MDPs, cost-relevant history summarized by state variable
- model dynamic inter-temporal choice + strategic interaction -> long popular framework

2. Challenges
- vs. single-agent RL: non-stationarity, conflicting interests, decentralized information
- theory lagged single-agent counterpart
- empirical successes (two examples) -> recent attention, theoretical advances on several axes (surveyed in Section 2)
- bulk of progress: finitely many states; much less known for general state spaces (real-world settings without finite models)

3. Setting
- decentralized MARL, standard Borel state spaces (includes finite, countably infinite, finite-dim vector spaces)
- no generative model, no offline data set; learn from in-game feedback, sequential interaction
- agents may not observe others' actions, still try to respond optimally
- want: individually rational algorithm + long-term system-wide stability, policies converge under self-play

4. Approach
- decentralized MARL algorithm for standard Borel state spaces + formal analysis
- extends Decentralized Q-learning (prior work) via state quantization
- care needed: quantization restricts policy class, may limit learning efficacy
- sufficient conditions on game -> arbitrarily small performance loss
- builds on quantized Q-learning results for single-agent MDPs with general state spaces

5. Exploration phases
- policies change only at prescribed times t_{0}<t_{1}<\dots, fixed during [t_{k},t_{k+1}-1], k\geq 0
- update times predetermined, common; no other coordination; all may change simultaneously or not
- no communication, no observing others' actions/costs, not even aware of other agents or game
- policy updates asymptotically optimal w.r.t. most recently observed environment
- joint policy dynamics for best-reply-based updates; convergence to equilibrium; weakly acyclic games
- other settings where self-play -> \epsilon -equilibrium policies

## Contributions
- Algorithm 1: decentralized MARL for general state spaces; Theorem 4.1: near-optimal updates under weak continuity of transition kernel + continuous cost
- Proposition 5.1: global joint policy dynamics of best-reply-based algorithms, convergence to equilibria
- Section 7: simulation study

## Organization
- Sec 2 related work; Sec 3 background; Sec 4 algorithm + results; Sec 5 policy dynamics; Sec 6 convergence + future work; Sec 7 simulations

Notation
- \mathbb{P}, \mathbb{E}; \mathcal{P}(S); \mathcal{P}(S^{\prime}|S); hat accent for quantization approximations

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) studies the learning dynamics of strategic agents that coexist in a shared environment, and it is one of the important frontiers of machine learning and control. In this paper we study MARL in stochastic games, which are also known as Markov games. These are a multi-agent generalization of Markov decision problems (MDPs) where the cost-relevant history of the system is summarized by a state variable. Because it can model both dynamic inter-temporal choice and strategic interaction, the stochastic games model has long been a popular framework for studying multi-agent learning.

Compared to single-agent reinforcement learning, MARL is difficult to analyze because of several challenges that are inherent to multi-agent systems, such as non-stationarity, conflicting interests, and decentralized information. So the fundamental understanding of multi-agent reinforcement learning theory has lagged behind the single-agent case. Partly because of a variety of impressive empirical successes, like those of one group and another, learning in stochastic games has recently attracted a lot of attention, and there have been theoretical advances along several research axes. We survey some of these advances in more detail in Section 2, where we observe that most of the theoretical progress in MARL has focused on games with finitely many states. Much less is known about learning in games with more general state spaces, which model various real-world settings that do not admit finite state space models.

In this paper we study decentralized multi-agent reinforcement learning in stochastic games with standard Borel state spaces, which include finite sets, countably infinite sets, and finite dimensional vector spaces as special cases. We are interested in the setting where there is no generative model available for sampling state and (joint) action feedback and no offline data set available to the players. Instead the players have to learn using in-game feedback, updating their estimates and adjusting their behaviour only as new information comes from sequential interaction with the environment. We keep decentralized settings in mind, where agents may not be able to observe the actions of other agents but must still try to respond optimally to the decision rules of others. In this context we want to propose an algorithm that can be justified from an individual rationality point of view, but that also has some long term guarantee of system-wide stability, with policies converging to some joint policy under self-play.

With these objectives in mind, we present a decentralized MARL algorithm for stochastic games with standard Borel state spaces and give a formal analysis of its properties. The algorithm extends the Decentralized Q-learning algorithm of prior work to settings with general state spaces by quantizing the state variable. This approach is natural, but it has to be implemented with care: when the state space is quantized, the algorithm designer artificially restricts the class of policies and may unintentionally limit how effective the learning agents are. We rigorously analyze this state space quantization and give sufficient conditions on the game that ensure the approach entails an arbitrarily small loss in performance. For this analysis we use recent theoretical advances in single-agent MDPs with general state spaces, building most prominently on the quantized Q-learning results of prior work.

- exploration phases: policies change only at prescribed times t_{0}<t_{1}<\dots, fixed during [t_{k},t_{k+1}-1], k\geq 0
- update times predetermined + common; no other coordination; agents may all change at t_{k} or not change
- no communication, no observing others' actions/costs, not even aware of others or of the game
- result: updates asymptotically optimal w.r.t. most recently observed environment
- also: joint policy dynamics for best-reply-based updates; convergence to equilibrium; weakly acyclic games; settings where self-play -> \epsilon -equilibrium policies

## Contributions:
- Algorithm 1 + Theorem 4.1: near-optimal updates under weak continuity of transition kernel and continuous cost
- Proposition 5.1: global joint policy-updating dynamics, convergence to equilibria
- Section 7: simulation study

## Organization
- Sec 2 related work; Sec 3 background; Sec 4 continuous-space extension + results; Sec 5 policy dynamics; Sec 6 equilibrium + future work; Sec 7 simulations

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) studies the learning dynamics of strategic agents that coexist in a shared environment, and it is one of the important frontiers of machine learning and control. In this paper we study MARL in stochastic games, which are also known as Markov games. These are a multi-agent generalization of Markov decision problems (MDPs) where the cost-relevant history of the system is summarized by a state variable. Because it can model both dynamic inter-temporal choice and strategic interaction, the stochastic games model has long been a popular framework for studying multi-agent learning.

Compared to single-agent reinforcement learning, MARL is difficult to analyze because of several challenges that are inherent to multi-agent systems, such as non-stationarity, conflicting interests, and decentralized information. So the fundamental understanding of multi-agent reinforcement learning theory has lagged behind the single-agent case. Partly because of a variety of impressive empirical successes, like those of one group and another, learning in stochastic games has recently attracted a lot of attention, and there have been theoretical advances along several research axes. We survey some of these advances in more detail in Section 2, where we observe that most of the theoretical progress in MARL has focused on games with finitely many states. Much less is known about learning in games with more general state spaces, which model various real-world settings that do not admit finite state space models.

In this paper we study decentralized multi-agent reinforcement learning in stochastic games with standard Borel state spaces, which include finite sets, countably infinite sets, and finite dimensional vector spaces as special cases. We are interested in the setting where there is no generative model available for sampling state and (joint) action feedback and no offline data set available to the players. Instead the players have to learn using in-game feedback, updating their estimates and adjusting their behaviour only as new information comes from sequential interaction with the environment. We keep decentralized settings in mind, where agents may not be able to observe the actions of other agents but must still try to respond optimally to the decision rules of others. In this context we want to propose an algorithm that can be justified from an individual rationality point of view, but that also has some long term guarantee of system-wide stability, with policies converging to some joint policy under self-play.

With these objectives in mind, we present a decentralized MARL algorithm for stochastic games with standard Borel state spaces and give a formal analysis of its properties. The algorithm extends the Decentralized Q-learning algorithm of prior work to settings with general state spaces by quantizing the state variable. This approach is natural, but it has to be implemented with care: when the state space is quantized, the algorithm designer artificially restricts the class of policies and may unintentionally limit how effective the learning agents are. We rigorously analyze this state space quantization and give sufficient conditions on the game that ensure the approach entails an arbitrarily small loss in performance. For this analysis we use recent theoretical advances in single-agent MDPs with general state spaces, building most prominently on the quantized Q-learning results of prior work.

The algorithm relies on the exploration phase technique, which requires that agents change their policies only at prescribed times, t_{0}<t_{1}<\dots, and hold their policies fixed during the intervals [t_{k},t_{k+1}-1], for k\geq 0. (So players do not change policies between update times.) The update times are predetermined and common to all agents, but apart from this no special coordination structure is assumed. In particular, all agents may change their policies at the same time at an update time t_{k}, or may choose not to change their policy. Besides this synchrony assumption, agents do not need to communicate, observe each other's actions or cost realizations, or even be aware of the other agents or that they are playing a game. Despite this decentralization, we show that the policy updates of our algorithm are asymptotically optimal for each agent with respect to the most recently observed environment.

Besides the near optimality of the policy updates from our algorithm, we also analyze the joint policy dynamics for a class of best-reply-based updates. For these algorithms we study convergence to equilibrium and characterize the convergence behaviour when the game has weakly acyclic structure. Finally, we describe additional settings where self-play of our algorithm drives the joint policy process to \epsilon -equilibrium policies.

## Contributions:

- In Algorithm 1 we propose a decentralized MARL algorithm for environments with general state spaces. In Theorem 4.1 we prove that the algorithm gives policy updates that are near-optimal with respect to each agent's observed environment, assuming weak continuity of the transition kernel and continuity of the cost function.

- In Proposition 5.1 we analyze theoretically the global joint policy-updating dynamics of a general class of best-reply-based algorithms and study convergence to equilibria.

- In Section 7 we present a simulation study that corroborates our theoretical study.

## Organization

The rest of the paper is structured as follows. Section 2 discusses related work on multi-agent reinforcement learning algorithms with theoretical guarantees. Section 3 gives the relevant background on modeling multi-agent environments. In Section 4 we propose a continuous-space extension of the decentralized multi-agent Q-learning algorithm and present the theoretical results that go with it. In Section 5 we derive a complete characterization of the global policy-updating dynamics of our algorithms. Section 6 discusses convergence to equilibrium and suggests lines of future research. Section 7 presents a simulation study of our algorithm.

Although this approach is natural, one must implement it with care: by quantizing the state space, the algorithm designer artificially restricts the class of policies and may unintentionally limit the efficacy of its learning agents. We rigorously analyze such a state space quantization, and we provide sufficient conditions on the game that ensure the approach entails an arbitrarily small loss in performance. To accomplish this analysis, we use recent theoretical advances in single-agent MDPs with general state spaces, building most prominently on the quantized Q-learning results of [7].

The algorithm presented here relies on the exploration phase technique, which requires that agents change their policies only at prescribed times, t_{0}<t_{1}<\dots, and hold their policies fixed during the intervals [t_{k},t_{k+1}-1], for k\geq 0. (That is, players do not change policies between update times.) The update times are predetermined and common to all agents, but outside of this no special coordination structure is assumed. In particular, all agents may change their policies simultaneously at an update time t_{k}, or may choose not to change their policy. Besides this assumption on synchrony, agents need not communicate, observe one another’s actions or cost realizations, or even be aware of the other agents or of the fact that they are playing a game. Despite this decentralization, we show that the policy updates of our algorithm are asymptotically optimal for each agent with respect to the most recently observed environment.

In addition to the near optimality of policy updates resulting from our algorithm, we also analyze the joint policy dynamics for a class of best-reply-based updates. For such algorithms, we study convergence to equilibrium and give a characterization of the convergence behaviour when the game admits weakly acyclic structure. Finally, we describe additional settings where self-play of our algorithm drives the joint policy process to \epsilon -equilibrium policies.

## Contributions:

- In Algorithm 1, we propose a decentralized MARL algorithm for environments with general state spaces. In Theorem 4.1, we prove that this algorithm yields policy updates which are near-optimal with respect to each agent’s observed environment, under the assumptions of weak continuity of the transition kernel and continuity of the cost function.

- In Proposition 5.1, we theoretically analyze the global joint policy-updating dynamics of a general class of best-reply-based algorithms and study convergence to equilibria.

- In Section 7 we present a simulation study that corroborates our theoretical study.

## Organization

The remainder of the paper is structured as follows. In Section 2 we discuss some related work on multi-agent reinforcement learning algorithms with theoretical guarantees. Section 3 gives the relevant background on modeling multi-agent environments. In Section 4 we propose a continuous-space extension of the decentralized multi-agent Q-learning algorithm and present our accompanying theoretical results. In Section 5 we derive a complete characterization of the global policy-updating dynamics of our algorithms. Section 6 discusses convergence to equilibrium and suggests lines of future research. Section 7 presents a simulation study of our algorithm.
